title: Why do firms default on their foreign currency loans? The case of Hungary
journal: Journal of International Money and Finance
summary_en: Hungarian firms borrowed heavily in foreign currency before the 2008 crisis; once the forint depreciated, many defaulted. Ongena, Schindele and Vonnák use Hungarian credit-registry data to ask which firms were most likely to default on FX loans, separating exchange-rate exposure, balance-sheet vulnerability, and bank-side risk-management practices. The paper provides a granular picture of FX-loan default determinants in a crisis episode that became the textbook case for emerging-market currency mismatch.
data_used: Hungarian credit-registry data linking firm-level loan terms (currency, maturity, interest rate) to borrowers' balance-sheet characteristics around the 2008 crisis. Default events tracked at the loan level. [Author summary based on the published title and known author work; the full abstract is not publicly accessible — verification by the editor against the published paper is recommended.]
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian financial-stability policy (MNB macroprudential framework, household and SME FX-exposure rules) and for emerging-market peers facing renewed dollarisation. The case study underpinned the post-2010 Hungarian FX-loan policy package (forintosítás for households, FX-loan restrictions for SMEs); the paper provides the empirical foundation linking firm-level FX exposure to default risk that remains central to macroprudential calibration.
